blocks.text: The Port Harcourt refinery takes in one dark, smelly liquid and sends out petrol, kerosene, diesel and bitumen. It does not use a single chemical reaction to do it. It uses one separation technique — fractional distillation — scaled up to the size of a tower.

blocks.markdown:
## Choose the method to match the difference

Every separation technique works by exploiting **one physical property in which the components differ**. Get into the habit of asking: *what is different about these two substances?* The answer names the method.

- Different particle size, one insoluble: **filtration**
- Different boiling points: **distillation** or **fractional distillation**
- Different solubility in the same solvent: **crystallisation** or **fractional crystallisation**
- Different adsorption on paper: **chromatography**
- One component sublimes: **sublimation**
- One component is magnetic: **magnetic separation**
- Different densities of two immiscible liquids: **separating funnel**

blocks.title: Filtrate and residue
blocks.text: In filtration the liquid that passes through the filter paper is the filtrate; the insoluble solid trapped on the paper is the residue. Examiners frequently ask you to name both, so learn the pair together.

blocks.markdown:
### Fractional distillation in more detail

When two liquids are miscible and their boiling points are close, simple distillation gives an impure product. A **fractionating column** packed with glass beads or fitted with plates is inserted between the flask and the condenser.

Vapour rising up the column repeatedly condenses and re-evaporates. Each cycle enriches the vapour in the more volatile component, so by the time vapour reaches the top it is almost pure. Ethanol (boiling point 78 degrees Celsius) distils over before water (100 degrees Celsius).

blocks.title: Separating a three-component mixture
blocks.prompt: A student is given a solid mixture of common salt, sand and ammonium chloride. Describe how to obtain all three components separately.

steps.text: Step 1 — Heat the mixture gently in an evaporating dish covered with an inverted funnel. Ammonium chloride sublimes and re-forms as a white solid on the cool funnel. Scrape it off. Salt and sand do not sublime, so they remain.
Step 2 — Add distilled water to the residue and stir. Sodium chloride dissolves; sand is insoluble.
Step 3 — Filter the suspension. Sand is the residue on the filter paper; wash it with distilled water and dry it in an oven.
Step 4 — Evaporate the filtrate over a water bath until the solution is saturated, then allow it to cool so that sodium chloride crystallises out. Filter and dry the crystals.
Each step relies on a different physical property: sublimation, then solubility, then crystallisation.

blocks.answer: Sublimation removes the ammonium chloride, filtration removes the sand, and evaporation followed by crystallisation recovers the sodium chloride.

blocks.markdown:
### Paper chromatography

A spot of the mixture is placed on a pencil **baseline** near the bottom of chromatography paper, which is then dipped in solvent so that the solvent level is *below* the baseline. As the solvent rises, components that are more soluble in the solvent and less strongly held by the paper travel further.

The retardation factor is

$R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by the spot}}{\text{distance moved by the solvent front}}$

$R_f$ is always between 0 and 1 and is constant for a given substance and solvent.

blocks.title: Two marks students lose every year
blocks.text: First, always draw the chromatography baseline in pencil — ink would dissolve and run. Second, in distillation the thermometer bulb must be level with the side arm so that it reads the temperature of the vapour entering the condenser, not the liquid in the flask.

points: Every separation exploits a physical property in which the components differ.
Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid, giving a residue and a filtrate.
Simple distillation recovers the solvent; fractional distillation separates miscible liquids with close boiling points.
Crystallisation purifies a solid whose solubility falls sharply as the solution cools.
Chromatography separates soluble coloured substances and is quantified by the Rf value.
